History:
• Chief complaint: New-onset dry, itchy, red skin on arms and hands.  
• Onset/duration: Began “a few days ago,” noted after a swimming session.  
• Course/progression: Persistent; coconut-butter application has not relieved itch.  
• Location: Bilateral arms and hands; no spread to chest, legs, or face.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies spots, fever, sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, urinary changes, or skin discharge/bleeding. Reports feeling tired but otherwise well; appetite and hydration normal.  
• Triggers/precipitating factors: Possible chlorine exposure from swimming; recent increased occupational stress (primary-school teacher, long hours).  
• Previous episodes: None.  

Past Medical History:
• Chronic illnesses: None reported.  
• Possible lactose intolerance (patient-reported, not confirmed).  
• Medications: Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive), dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: No drug/food allergies reported; lactose intolerance noted.  
• Family history: Father – asthma; Mother – hay fever; no family skin disorders.  
• Social: Lives alone; non-smoker; minimal alcohol; no recreational drug use.

Physical Examination:
(No in-person exam; video consultation only.)  
• General: Appears well; alert and oriented.  
• Skin (patient-reported): Diffuse dry, erythematous, pruritic patches on hands and arms; no pustules, vesicles, or cracking; no bleeding or discharge.  
• Systemic review (patient-reported): Afebrile; no GI or GU complaints; no respiratory symptoms.

Impression:
Likely irritant/contact dermatitis, possibly triggered by pool chlorine and exacerbated by stress.

Management Plan:
• Education: Provided patient information leaflet on dermatitis.  
• Topical therapy: Prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream (potency and regimen not documented) plus regular use of emollients; advised liberal application throughout the day.  
• Symptomatic relief: Suggested over-the-counter oral antihistamines (e.g., chlorphenamine, loratadine) for pruritus.  
• Analgesia: Advised paracetamol unnecessary at present.  
• Follow-up: If no improvement within one week, return for re-evaluation.

Patient Summary:
26-year-old teacher developed a pruritic, erythematous rash on hands/arms shortly after swimming. No systemic illness. Presentation consistent with contact dermatitis; started on steroid cream, emollients, and optional antihistamines. Will reassess in one week if symptoms persist.

Key Takeaways:
• Apply steroid cream and emollient to affected areas several times daily.  
• Take an OTC antihistamine if itch interferes with comfort or sleep.  
• Seek review next week or sooner for worsening, spreading, or infected-looking skin.

Next Steps:
• Monitor response over the next 7 days.  
• If inadequate improvement, arrange in-person examination; consider stronger topical steroid, patch testing, or dermatology referral.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing expected elements: No vital signs, no direct physical examination findings, allergy list incomplete (only lactose intolerance noted).  
• Internal conflicts: None identified.  
• Transcript quality: Clear audio with minor pauses; no significant inaudible sections.
